y-m-53-01.title: If we put in numbers for the letters, are the two expressions always equal?
y-m-53-01.topic: Expressions with letters: when two expressions are equal, and counterexamples
y-m-53-01.goal: Pick the values that break the claim 'it holds for all values' and use them as counterexamples, then collect the values for which it holds by chance and guess their common condition.
y-m-53-01.material: Sua wrote this in her notebook. “For any real numbers a and b, (a+b)² and a²+b² are equal.” Here (a+b)² means 'the square of a plus b,' and a²+b² means 'a squared plus b squared.' Find out whether this claim is always right, and if not, for which values it is right.
y-m-53-01.thinking.0: Sorting out counterexamples and cases that are right by chance
y-m-53-01.thinking.1: Guessing the condition from examples where it holds
y-m-53-01.thinking.2: Telling 'always' apart from 'only under some condition'
y-m-53-01.prereq.0: This assumes basic high school math learning (a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations). H1 is only a difficulty and support level for production assignment; it does not mean the curriculum places this subject in Grade 10, and school arrangements vary.
y-m-53-01.prereq.1: Putting numbers in for letters to find the value of an expression (middle school level)
y-m-53-01.prereq.2: The meaning of a square: a² is the number you get by multiplying a by itself twice
y-m-53-01.s.s1.prompt: Pick all the tests that show Sua's claim does not always hold. (Put the values below in for a and b and compare the values of the two expressions.)
y-m-53-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each test, calculate the values of (a+b)² and a²+b² separately and write them side by side.
y-m-53-01.s.s1.hint.1: Sort the tests into those where the two values are equal and those where they are different.
y-m-53-01.s.s1.r.a: These are values where the two expressions come out equal. Values that come out equal neither support nor break the claim.
y-m-53-01.s.s1.r.b: You picked the tests by whether the values of the two expressions differ. If even one value disagrees, 'always' is broken.
y-m-53-01.s.s1.r.c: Even if you gather values that come out equal, you cannot say 'always.' You have to look for values that disagree.
y-m-53-01.s.s1.r.d: You also tested values whose sum is 0. Without putting values in, you cannot see the difference between the two expressions.
y-m-53-01.s.s1.explain: If a=1, b=2, then (1+2)²=9 and 1²+2²=5, which differ, and if a=3, b=−3, then 0²=0 and 9+9=18, which differ. On the other hand, for a=2, b=0 and a=0, b=5, the two expressions are equal. No matter how many values that come out equal you gather, they do not guarantee 'always,' and a single different value breaks the claim.
y-m-53-01.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 different (a, b) for which Sua's claim is right by chance, that is, the values of the two expressions are equal. Exclude the case where a and b are both 0, and keep the size of both numbers at 100 or less. (Swapping a and b counts as the same example.)
y-m-53-01.s.s2.hint.0: Look at what a and b have in common in the tests that already came out equal (values like a=2, b=0).
y-m-53-01.s.s2.hint.1: Put the newly chosen values directly into the two expressions, check that they come out equal, and then enter them.
y-m-53-01.s.s2.ok.c1: It is not the case where both are 0.
y-m-53-01.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b are both 0. At least one of them must be a nonzero value.
y-m-53-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The sizes (absolute values) of a and b must be 100 or less.
y-m-53-01.s.s2.ok.c3: The values of the two expressions are equal.
y-m-53-01.s.s2.fail.c3: For these values, (a+b)² and a²+b² are different. Calculate the two values separately and compare them.
y-m-53-01.s.s2.explain: Since (a+b)²=a²+2ab+b², for the two expressions to be equal, 2ab=0 must hold. So they are equal only for values where one of a or b is 0, like 3 and 0, or 0 and −4.
y-m-53-01.s.s3.prompt: What would you say to Sua? Using the examples you just gathered as evidence, say that the claim is not always true, and guess and write the condition for when the two expressions are equal.
y-m-53-01.s.s3.hint.0: Use one test from s1 above where the values came out different as a counterexample, then go on to talk about the examples where they came out equal.
y-m-53-01.s.s3.hint.1: Look at which of a and b is 0 in common among the examples that came out equal.
y-m-53-01.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. It's not always true. ... They are equal only when ...
y-m-53-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate directly whether the two expressions really come out equal (or different) for the values you gave?
y-m-53-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say both 'it is not always' and 'in some cases they are equal'?
y-m-53-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: If you stated a condition, can you make one more example that fits that condition and test it?
y-m-53-01.s.s3.model.0: It's not always true. If you put in 1 and 2, you get 9 and 5, so they differ. If one of the two is 0, like 3 and 0, the two expressions are equal. When you expand (a+b)² you get a²+2ab+b², so it seems they are equal only when ab=0.
y-m-53-01.s.s3.model.1: What Sua said is not right. If you put in 3 and −3, you get 0 and 18, which differ. They seem to be equal only when the product is 0, like when a or b is 0.
y-m-53-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: It is also fine to guess the condition from examples only, without expanding.

y-m-53-02.title: The answer that disappeared during the solution
y-m-53-02.topic: Solving equations: solutions missed during rewriting
y-m-53-02.goal: Find a line in the solution that was written without justification, check by substituting into the original expression that this line can make a solution disappear, and rewrite it correctly.
y-m-53-02.material: x is a real number. Jihu solved the equation x(x−3)=2x and wrote the answer as below. (x(x−3) means 'x times x minus 3.')
y-m-53-02.thinking.0: Finding in which line a condition was assumed
y-m-53-02.thinking.1: Checking by substituting into the original expression
y-m-53-02.thinking.2: Fixing the solution without missing a solution
y-m-53-02.prereq.0: This assumes basic high school math learning (a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations). H1 is only a difficulty and support level for production assignment; it does not mean the curriculum places this subject in Grade 10, and school arrangements vary.
y-m-53-02.prereq.1: Solving linear equations, and the basics of reading an expression whose product is 0
y-m-53-02.prereq.2: Checking a solution of an equation by putting it into the original expression
y-m-53-02.s.s1.prompt: Pick one line in Jihu's solution that was written without justification.
y-m-53-02.s.s1.hint.0: Ask one by one under what condition each line can come from the line just before it.
y-m-53-02.s.s1.hint.1: Pick a few values and check whether the change in line 2 is a change you can make no matter what number is put in for x.
y-m-53-02.s.s1.line.1: Dividing both sides by x gives x−3=2.
y-m-53-02.s.s1.line.3: So the only solution of this equation is x=5.
y-m-53-02.s.s1.explain: To divide both sides by x in line 2, x must not be 0. x could be 0, but this was not examined separately. As a result, the 'only one' in line 4 is also unjustified. Putting x=0 into the original expression gives 0=0, so one solution disappeared.
y-m-53-02.s.s2.prompt: We want to check whether x=0 is also a solution. What is the most reliable method?
y-m-53-02.s.s2.hint.0: First decide whether the expression you put the value into is the 'original expression' or the 'changed expression.'
y-m-53-02.s.s2.hint.1: Put in x=0 and x=5 and calculate the left side and the right side separately.
y-m-53-02.s.s2.o.a: Put x=0 and x=5 into the expression after dividing, x−3=2, and compare both sides
y-m-53-02.s.s2.r.a: If you put it into the changed expression, you only learn the answer for the changed expression. Whether it is the same as the original expression has to be checked separately.
y-m-53-02.s.s2.o.b: x=5 came out, so we consider that there are no other solutions
y-m-53-02.s.s2.r.b: You are treating it as finished once you get one. The other values have not been tested yet.
y-m-53-02.s.s2.o.c: 0 is a number you must not divide by, so we remove it from the solutions
y-m-53-02.s.s2.r.c: Division being impossible and the original expression holding are separate matters.
y-m-53-02.s.s2.o.d: Put x=0 and x=5 into the original expression and compare both sides
y-m-53-02.s.s2.r.d: This is the method of putting values directly into the original expression. It is a check you can use no matter what solving process was followed.
y-m-53-02.s.s2.explain: If you put values directly into the original expression, it can be checked regardless of the solving process. If x=0 then 0=0, and if x=5 then 10=10, so both hold.
y-m-53-02.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite from the start a solution that finds all the solutions of x(x−3)=2x. Also say what Jihu missed.
y-m-53-02.s.s3.hint.0: First decide for which value Jihu's line 2 does not hold, and handle that value separately.
y-m-53-02.s.s3.hint.1: Try moving the terms so that one side becomes 0 and see what form it takes.
y-m-53-02.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. Jihu missed ... The solutions are ...
y-m-53-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you put 0 and 5 into the original expression and check that both hold?
y-m-53-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you handle the case where division is impossible (x=0) separately, or use another method that solves without dividing?
y-m-53-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about what justification is needed in order to say 'these are the only solutions'?
y-m-53-02.s.s3.model.0: If you move terms to get x(x−3)−2x=0, it becomes x(x−5)=0, so x=0 or x=5. Jihu divided by x even though x could be 0, so he missed x=0.
y-m-53-02.s.s3.model.1: When x=0 you cannot divide by x, so look at it separately. If x=0 then 0=0, so it is a solution, and if x is not 0 then x−3=2, so x=5. So the solutions are 0 and 5.

y-m-53-03.title: How many answers does the equation have?
y-m-53-03.topic: Quadratic equations: the number of real roots and the coefficient k
y-m-53-03.goal: Learn that for a quadratic equation with a letter in its coefficient, the number of real roots changes depending on the value of the letter, state the information needed (the range of k), and find the boundary values yourself.
y-m-53-03.material: k is a real constant, and x is a real number. Consider the equation x²+kx+4=0. (x² means 'x squared.') Find out how many real roots, that is, solutions where x is a real number, this equation has.
y-m-53-03.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
y-m-53-03.thinking.1: Splitting into cases and stating the conclusion together with its condition
y-m-53-03.prereq.0: This assumes basic high school math learning (a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations). H1 is only a difficulty and support level for production assignment; it does not mean the curriculum places this subject in Grade 10, and school arrangements vary.
y-m-53-03.prereq.1: The experience of putting in values to see whether there is an x that makes the quadratic expression x²+px+q equal to 0
y-m-53-03.prereq.2: We think within the real numbers (complex numbers are not used)
y-m-53-03.s.s1.prompt: Without knowing the value of k, can you say the number of real roots of this equation as a single number?
y-m-53-03.s.s1.hint.0: Put two or three different numbers in for k and check one by one whether there are roots.
y-m-53-03.s.s1.hint.1: If there is a k for which the number of roots is different, it means more information is needed.
y-m-53-03.s.s1.o.a: No matter which real number k is, there are always 2 real roots
y-m-53-03.s.s1.r.a: How many values did you try for k? When k=1, check whether there is an x that makes x²+x+4 equal to 0.
y-m-53-03.s.s1.o.b: We have to know the value (range) of k to decide
y-m-53-03.s.s1.r.b: You noticed that information is lacking and even said what more information is needed. If the coefficient changes, the expression changes too.
y-m-53-03.s.s1.o.c: No matter which real number k is, there are no real roots
y-m-53-03.s.s1.r.c: Put in x=−1 and see whether it is a solution when k=5. If you conclude from one or two values, you miss some cases.
y-m-53-03.s.s1.o.d: Regardless of k, there is always exactly 1 real root
y-m-53-03.s.s1.r.d: Put in k=5 or k=1 and count the number of roots directly.
y-m-53-03.s.s1.explain: If k=5, then x²+5x+4=(x+1)(x+4), so there are two real roots, −1 and −4, and if k=1, then x²+x+4 is always positive, so there are no real roots. The number of roots changes with k, so we need to know the value or range of k.
y-m-53-03.s.s2.prompt: Enter 2 different values of k for which there is exactly 1 real root (the case where two equal roots overlap).
y-m-53-03.s.s2.hint.0: The roots overlap into one only when x²+kx+4 becomes the square of something. Write the square form (x+m)² as an expression that starts with x².
y-m-53-03.s.s2.hint.1: Test both the case where m is positive and the case where m is negative.
y-m-53-03.s.s2.ok.c1: For this k there is exactly one real root.
y-m-53-03.s.s2.fail.c1: For this k there is not exactly one real root. Look at whether x²+kx+4 takes the form (x+something)².
y-m-53-03.s.s2.explain: If k=4, then x²+4x+4=(x+2)², and if k=−4, then x²−4x+4=(x−2)², so each has one real root. These two are the only k for which there is one root.
y-m-53-03.s.s3.prompt: Write by splitting into cases how the number of real roots changes depending on the value of k. Also use k=5 and k=1 from before as examples.
y-m-53-03.s.s3.hint.0: Put in k=0, k=2, k=3, k=5, k=6 and so on, and organize in a table whether there are roots.
y-m-53-03.s.s3.hint.1: Find in the table about where the number of roots changes, and check by putting in that value directly.
y-m-53-03.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If k is ..., then ...; if k is ..., then ...
y-m-53-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you distinguish for which k each of the three cases (none, one, two) happens?
y-m-53-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check with an example like k=4 why there is one root at the boundary value?
y-m-53-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also examine negative k (for example −5) in the same way?
y-m-53-03.s.s3.model.0: If k is greater than 4 or less than −4 there are 2 real roots, if k=4 or k=−4 there is 1 (a double root), and if −4<k<4 there are no real roots. For example, if k=5, then x²+5x+4=(x+1)(x+4) has two roots, −1 and −4, and if k=1, then x²+x+4 is always positive, so there are no roots.
y-m-53-03.s.s3.model.1: Splitting into cases: when |k|>4 there are two different real roots, when |k|=4 there is one equal root (a double root), and when |k|<4 there are no real roots. k=5 is the case with two, and k=1 is the case with none.
y-m-53-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: An expression written all at once with the absolute value symbol is also valid.

y-m-53-04.title: Reading the same inequality in two ways
y-m-53-04.topic: Linear inequalities with absolute values: reading as distance and splitting into cases
y-m-53-04.goal: Compare reading an absolute value inequality as a distance on the number line with splitting into cases, and find and fix the line in the case-splitting solution where a condition was left out.
y-m-53-04.material: x is a real number. Yeongha and Bora read the inequality |x−3|≤2 ('the absolute value of x minus 3 is less than or equal to 2') in different ways. Yeongha read it as “the distance between 3 and x on the number line is 2 or less,” and Bora solved it by “splitting into the case where x−3 is 0 or more and the case where it is less than 0.”
y-m-53-04.thinking.0: Comparing the strengths and weaknesses of the two solving methods
y-m-53-04.thinking.1: Checking whether the condition is written together in each case
y-m-53-04.thinking.2: Applying the method to another inequality (the case with the opposite sign)
y-m-53-04.prereq.0: This assumes basic high school math learning (a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations). H1 is only a difficulty and support level for production assignment; it does not mean the curriculum places this subject in Grade 10, and school arrangements vary.
y-m-53-04.prereq.1: The meaning of the distance between two points on a number line and the meaning of absolute value (|a| is the distance from 0 to a)
y-m-53-04.s.s1.prompt: Pick all the x that satisfy |x−3|≤2. Test the values directly using Yeongha's reading.
y-m-53-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each value, find the absolute value of the value minus 3 (the distance from 3) and compare it with 2.
y-m-53-04.s.s1.hint.1: If there is a value whose distance is exactly 2, read again whether the inequality sign is ≤ or <.
y-m-53-04.s.s1.r.a: Find the distance between 3 and 0 and compare it with 2. Did you just feel that it was close without comparing?
y-m-53-04.s.s1.r.b: You compared whether the boundary value is also included. If the inequality sign is '≤' (less than or equal to), points whose distance is exactly 2 are also included.
y-m-53-04.s.s1.r.c: This is a point 1 away from 3 to the right. You found the distance and compared it with the standard.
y-m-53-04.s.s1.r.d: You judged by the inequality sign whether to include the boundary value. The right boundary works in the same way.
y-m-53-04.s.s1.r.e: This is a point whose distance is greater than the standard. Find the distance between 3 and 6 and compare it with 2.
y-m-53-04.s.s1.explain: The distances of x=1, 4, 5 from 3 are 2, 1, 2 respectively, all 2 or less. For x=0 and 6, the distance is 3, which exceeds the standard. The solution is the segment on the number line extending 2 to each side of 3, that is, 1≤x≤5.
y-m-53-04.s.s2.prompt: Pick one line in Bora's solution process where the justification is lacking.
y-m-53-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write the result you found in each case together with the condition for that case.
y-m-53-04.s.s2.hint.1: Put x=10 into the finished solution and test whether the inequality holds.
y-m-53-04.s.s2.line.0: When x−3≥0, that is x≥3, |x−3|=x−3, so x−3≤2, that is x≤5.
y-m-53-04.s.s2.line.1: When x−3<0, that is x<3, |x−3|=−(x−3), so −(x−3)≤2, that is x≥1.
y-m-53-04.s.s2.line.2: Combining the results of the two cases and writing 'x≤5 or x≥1' gives all real numbers.
y-m-53-04.s.s2.line.3: Therefore the solution of the inequality is all real numbers.
y-m-53-04.s.s2.explain: In line 3, the result of each case must be seen together with the condition of that case. The first case has x≥3 and x≤5, so 3≤x≤5; the second case has x<3 and x≥1, so 1≤x<3; and combined, 1≤x≤5. The 'all real numbers' in line 4 is also wrong, because at x=10, |10−3|=7>2.
y-m-53-04.s.s3.prompt: Read it as a distance like Yeongha, find the solution of |x−3|≥2, and say what is good about reading it as a distance in this problem.
y-m-53-04.s.s3.hint.0: Mark 3 on the number line and plot the two points that are 2 away from 3.
y-m-53-04.s.s3.hint.1: Pick one point to test whether 'distance 2 or more' is between the two plotted points or outside them.
y-m-53-04.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. The distance from 3 is 2 or more, so ...
y-m-53-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check whether the inequality holds at the boundaries 1 and 5 of the two ranges you wrote?
y-m-53-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say what becomes easier when you use the number line picture, unlike the solution that splits into cases?
y-m-53-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you use 'and' (both) and 'or' (either one) correctly and separately?
y-m-53-04.s.s3.model.0: These are the numbers whose distance from 3 is 2 or more, so x≤1 or x≥5. You can put 1 and 5 on the number line and look at the outside parts, so you do not need to split into cases.
y-m-53-04.s.s3.model.1: x is 2 or more away from 3, so x is 1 or less or 5 or more. If you read it as a distance, the solution is visible right away from the number line picture, and there is less worry about leaving out a condition.

y-m-53-05.title: Can we find the prices from three receipts?
y-m-53-05.topic: Systems of linear equations: does the new information decide the solution?
y-m-53-05.goal: Learn that having one more equation does not necessarily decide the solution, and make up on your own a condition that counts as new information.
y-m-53-05.material: At a stationery store, let the price of one pencil be x원 and the price of one eraser be y원. x and y are natural numbers, and the price list cannot be seen. Receipts are revealed one at a time. (The actual values are not told until the end.)
y-m-53-05.thinking.0: Revising or keeping a judgment as information grows
y-m-53-05.thinking.1: Telling the number of equations apart from the amount of information
y-m-53-05.thinking.2: Designing a new condition that decides the solution
y-m-53-05.prereq.0: This assumes basic high school math learning (a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations). H1 is only a difficulty and support level for production assignment; it does not mean the curriculum places this subject in Grade 10, and school arrangements vary.
y-m-53-05.prereq.1: Writing a linear equation with two unknowns and checking it by putting in values
y-m-53-05.s.s1.prompt: Receipts are revealed one at a time. Each time, choose your judgment about whether the price of one pencil can be known.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.hint.0: For each receipt, find two or more pairs of (x, y) that fit, and check whether the pairs you already found also fit the new receipt.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the ratio of counts (pencils : erasers) of the new receipt with the earlier receipt.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.0.info: Receipt ①: 2 pencils and 3 erasers cost 1900원. (2x+3y=1900)
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: Can we decide the price x of one pencil?
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.0.after: Both x=800, y=100 and x=500, y=300 satisfy receipt ① (1600+300=1900, 1000+900=1900). So x is not decided as a single value. However, since y is a natural number, we can say the range 2x<1900, that is, x<950.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You assumed that the pencil and the eraser cost the same. The receipt has no such information.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is not decided as one value. There are several pairs (x, y) that fit the receipt
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You checked whether there are several pairs of values that fit the receipt.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We do not know the exact value, but we can say that x is less than 950원
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Even though it cannot be decided, you found the range that can be stated. You used the condition that y is a natural number.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.0.o.d: There is a receipt, so we can decide it. We only need to calculate
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Whether one equation can decide two unknowns has to be judged after putting in values.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.1.info: Receipt ②: 4 pencils and 6 erasers cost 3800원. (4x+6y=3800)
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: If we combine this receipt too, can we decide x?
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.1.after: ② is the same as ① with both sides multiplied by 2, so x=800, y=100 and x=500, y=300 still both fit. Even with two equations, the values are not decided if there is no new information. Keeping the earlier judgment is the right thing.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: We can decide it. There are two equations now, so we can solve it
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You only counted the number of equations. Check whether the two equations are different pieces of information.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: We cannot decide it. Receipt ② has different values, so it is wrong
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Whether ② is wrong has to be checked by putting in values. Calculate ② using the pairs of values for ①.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: We still cannot decide it. ② is twice ①, so there is no new information
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You compared how ② is related to ①. You examined whether it is new information.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.1.o.d: We can decide it. It is a larger amount, so it is more accurate
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.1.r.d: A larger amount does not make it more accurate. The condition has to be different.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.2.info: Receipt ③: 1 pencil and 2 erasers cost 1000원. (x+2y=1000)
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: If both ① and ③ are right, what is the price of one pencil?
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.2.after: ③ has a different ratio of counts from ①, so it is new information. Putting x=1000−2y from ③ into ① gives 2000−4y+3y=1900, y=100, x=800. Check: 2×800+3×100=1900, 800+2×100=1000. Now the values are decided as single values.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: If x=500, then y=300 from ①. Calculate ③ with those values.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is a value checked by putting it into both ① and ③. It does not matter whether you use substitution or making a table.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Put x=600 into ① and check whether y becomes a natural number.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Compare whether the ratio in ③ is the same as in ①. If it is not the same ratio, it is new information.
y-m-53-05.s.s1.reflect: If you did not change your judgment when ② arrived but did change it at ③, what is the difference between the two cases? How are the number of equations and the amount of information different?
y-m-53-05.s.s2.prompt: The actual values are 800원 for a pencil and 100원 for an eraser. Make 2 new receipts (a pencils, b erasers, total c원) with different ratios that, together with ①, decide x and y as single values, and enter them. a and b are integers from 0 to 20, and they are not both 0.
y-m-53-05.s.s2.hint.0: First decide a and b, then calculate the total with the actual prices (800원 for a pencil, 100원 for an eraser) to decide c.
y-m-53-05.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the a:b you chose is the same ratio as ①'s 2:3, and if it is the same ratio, change to different a and b.
y-m-53-05.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b are integers from 0 to 20, and they cannot both be 0.
y-m-53-05.s.s2.ok.c2: It matches the total calculated with the actual prices.
y-m-53-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The total does not match the actual prices (800원 for a pencil, 100원 for an eraser). The receipt is wrong.
y-m-53-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The ratio of counts is different from ①.
y-m-53-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The ratio of counts is the same as ①, so it cannot be new information. It can be made by doubling or tripling ①.
y-m-53-05.s.s2.explain: If the ratio of pencils to erasers is different from ①'s 2:3 and the receipt matches the actual prices, then combined with ① the values are decided. Examples are (1, 2, 1000), (1, 1, 900), (3, 0, 2400). (4, 6, 3800), with ratio 2:3, is the same information as ①, so it does not work.
y-m-53-05.s.s2.because.prompt: In one or two sentences, compare with ① and write why the receipt you made, when used together with ①, decides the values.
y-m-53-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Read again the values or expressions you found in the earlier steps, and think about why they turn out that way.
y-m-53-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: First write the reason that comes to mind as one sentence in the form '... so ...,' and then polish it.
y-m-53-05.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g. ① is ..., but my receipt is ..., so ...
y-m-53-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the counts of ① (2 pencils, 3 erasers) with the counts of your receipt using numbers?
y-m-53-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say why your receipt cannot be made by doubling or tripling ①?
y-m-53-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you calculate again whether the total matches the actual prices?
y-m-53-05.s.s2.because.model.0: In ① the ratio of pencils to erasers is 2:3, but my receipt is 1:2, so the ratio is different. So it is new information that cannot be made by doubling or tripling ①.
y-m-53-05.s.s2.because.model.1: My receipt has 3 pencils and 0 erasers, so the price of a pencil is decided right away. It is different information from ①, so when the two are combined, x and y are decided as single values.

y-m-53-06.title: Making an equation whose two roots are integers
y-m-53-06.topic: Quadratic equations: designing equations with integer roots
y-m-53-06.goal: Judge what can be said about the signs of the roots from the signs of the coefficients alone, design quadratic equations that fit the conditions yourself, and explain the reason.
y-m-53-06.material: x is a real number. Consider the equation x²+bx+c=0 made with integers b and c. In this task we deal only with the case where b and c are both positive.
y-m-53-06.thinking.0: Making several answers within the conditions
y-m-53-06.thinking.1: Inferring the signs of the roots from the signs of the coefficients
y-m-53-06.thinking.2: Checking on your own that the examples you made satisfy the conditions
y-m-53-06.prereq.0: This assumes basic high school math learning (a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations). H1 is only a difficulty and support level for production assignment; it does not mean the curriculum places this subject in Grade 10, and school arrangements vary.
y-m-53-06.prereq.1: The experience of finding or checking the roots of a quadratic equation of the form x²+bx+c
y-m-53-06.prereq.2: Checking the solutions of a quadratic equation by putting them into the original expression
y-m-53-06.s.s1.prompt: When b and c are both positive, what statement about the roots of this equation is appropriate?
y-m-53-06.s.s1.hint.0: When you put positive numbers like 1, 2, 3 in for x, write whether each of the three terms of the expression (x², bx, c) is positive or negative.
y-m-53-06.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether the sum can be 0 when all three terms are positive.
y-m-53-06.s.s1.o.a: There is always one positive root
y-m-53-06.s.s1.r.a: Put in a few positive numbers for x and check whether the value of x²+bx+c becomes 0.
y-m-53-06.s.s1.o.b: If there are roots, they are one positive and one negative
y-m-53-06.s.s1.r.b: Think about what sign the product of the two roots would have if one is positive and one is negative.
y-m-53-06.s.s1.o.c: There cannot be a positive root
y-m-53-06.s.s1.r.c: You examined the sign of each term of the expression when x is positive. You inferred the signs of the roots from the signs of the coefficients.
y-m-53-06.s.s1.o.d: We cannot say anything about the roots from b and c alone
y-m-53-06.s.s1.r.d: If you make two or three concrete pairs of b and c and find the roots, you may see something they have in common.
y-m-53-06.s.s1.explain: If x>0, then x², bx, and c are all positive, so x²+bx+c>0. Therefore there is no positive x that makes it 0. If there are roots, they are all 0 or less, and since c>0, 0 is not a root either, so the roots are all negative.
y-m-53-06.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different equations x²+bx+c=0 in which b and c are both positive and which have two different integer roots, and enter b and c. (b is a positive integer 30 or less, c is a positive integer 200 or less)
y-m-53-06.s.s2.hint.0: Decide the two roots first and make the expression that has those roots backward.
y-m-53-06.s.s2.hint.1: Put the roots into the expression you made to check that it becomes 0, and also check that the two roots are different.
y-m-53-06.s.s2.ok.c1: b and c are positive integers that fit the conditions.
y-m-53-06.s.s2.fail.c1: b must be a positive integer from 1 to 30, and c a positive integer from 1 to 200.
y-m-53-06.s.s2.ok.c2: There are two different real roots.
y-m-53-06.s.s2.fail.c2: Two different real roots do not occur. It may be a case where the roots overlap or there are none.
y-m-53-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The roots are not integers. Find the two roots and change b and c so that they become integers.
y-m-53-06.s.s2.explain: If you decide the roots first, like −1 and −6, and expand (x+1)(x+6)=x²+7x+6, then b=7 and c=6. For example, (5, 6) has roots −2, −3; (7, 12) has roots −3, −4; (6, 8) has roots −2, −4. b=2, c=1 does not work because it has only the single equal root −1.
y-m-53-06.s.s3.prompt: The integer roots of the equations you just made must all have been negative. Write why, when b and c are positive, there cannot be a positive root. (You may explain by putting numbers into the expression, or by the sum and product of the two roots.)
y-m-53-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write down the signs of the three terms of the expression one by one when x is positive, and say whether the sum can be 0.
y-m-53-06.s.s3.hint.1: For one of the expressions you just made, find the sum and product of the two roots and compare them with b and c.
y-m-53-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation actually use the condition that b and c are positive?
y-m-53-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Do you know why the case where x is 0 or negative is not a problem?
y-m-53-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: If you apply your explanation to the three expressions you made, do the roots come out negative?
y-m-53-06.s.s3.model.0: If x is positive, then x², bx, and c are all positive, so x²+bx+c cannot be 0. So there is no positive root, and all the roots are negative.
y-m-53-06.s.s3.model.1: The sum of the two roots is −b, which is negative, and the product is c, which is positive, so the two roots have the same sign. Since the sum is negative, both are negative.
y-m-53-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: An explanation using the relation between sum and product is also valid. Even if you do not know this relation yet, an explanation by substituting is enough.

y-m-53-07.title: They are equal at three values, so are they always equal?
y-m-53-07.topic: Whether expressions are identical: how many values must be tested to be enough?
y-m-53-07.goal: Judge whether the fact that two expressions are equal at a few values is enough evidence for 'equal at all values,' and find the line in the argument that jumps ahead and state what kind of evidence is needed.
y-m-53-07.material: x is a real number. Minjae put −1, 0, and 1 in for x to compare the two expressions x³ and x, and the values of the two expressions were the same all three times. So he said, “For any number x, x³=x.” (x³ means 'x cubed.')
y-m-53-07.thinking.0: Judging whether the evidence is enough
y-m-53-07.thinking.1: Finding the jump in an argument
y-m-53-07.thinking.2: Telling apart checking examples and a general explanation
y-m-53-07.prereq.0: This assumes basic high school math learning (a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations). H1 is only a difficulty and support level for production assignment; it does not mean the curriculum places this subject in Grade 10, and school arrangements vary.
y-m-53-07.prereq.1: Putting numbers in for letters to find the value of an expression
y-m-53-07.prereq.2: x³ means the number you get by multiplying x three times
y-m-53-07.s.s1.prompt: Which is an appropriate judgment about Minjae's conclusion “For any number x, x³=x”?
y-m-53-07.s.s1.hint.0: Pick two or three values other than −1, 0, 1 and calculate the values of the two expressions separately.
y-m-53-07.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether any of the values you calculated came out different for the two expressions.
y-m-53-07.s.s1.o.a: We only checked at three values, so the evidence is not enough. We need to test more
y-m-53-07.s.s1.r.a: You pointed out that there are values not tested. You distinguished how far the conclusion has been confirmed.
y-m-53-07.s.s1.o.b: They were the same at all three values, so the evidence is enough
y-m-53-07.s.s1.r.b: Check whether the fact that the three values were the same carries over to values that were not tested.
y-m-53-07.s.s1.o.c: It may be true, but we can only say so after putting in other values like x=2
y-m-53-07.s.s1.r.c: You left open the possibility but put off the judgment. The next action is to look for a value that does not match.
y-m-53-07.s.s1.o.d: They are the same at three values, so x³=x does not hold for values other than −1, 0, 1
y-m-53-07.s.s1.r.d: Having values where they were the same and not holding for other values are separate things. The other values have not been tested yet.
y-m-53-07.s.s1.explain: If you put in x=2, then x³=8 and x=2, so they differ. Being the same at three values does not mean being the same at all values. If one value does not match, 'for any number' is broken.
y-m-53-07.s.s1.acc.0: A judgment that leaves open the possibility that it is true and says to test other values is also valid. The key point is that this evidence alone cannot settle the conclusion.
y-m-53-07.s.s2.prompt: Below is an explanation that Minjae's friend continued to write about x³=x. Pick one line that jumps ahead without evidence.
y-m-53-07.s.s2.hint.0: For each line, write in one sentence what evidence it came from in the lines just before.
y-m-53-07.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the evidence needed for the word 'only' is written before it.
y-m-53-07.s.s2.line.0: If you put in x=2, then x³=8 and x=2, so the values of the two expressions are different.
y-m-53-07.s.s2.line.1: Therefore x³=x is not an expression that holds for all x.
y-m-53-07.s.s2.line.2: However, at x=−1, 0, 1 the two expressions are equal, so these three numbers are solutions of the equation x³=x.
y-m-53-07.s.s2.line.3: Therefore the solutions of x³=x are only the three, −1, 0, 1.
y-m-53-07.s.s2.explain: To say 'only three' in line 4, you must show that other numbers are not solutions. The fact that a few tested values are solutions does not tell us there are no other solutions. (If you rewrite the expression in the form x(x−1)(x+1)=0, you can show that these three numbers are all of the solutions, but that is not the evidence in this line.) Lines 1 to 3 are things confirmed by direct calculation.
y-m-53-07.s.s3.prompt: Explain to Minjae. What is the difference between 'the two expressions are equal at a few values' and 'the two expressions are equal for all x'?
y-m-53-07.s.s3.hint.0: Try making how the values of the two expressions come out when you put in x=2 the starting point of your discussion.
y-m-53-07.s.s3.hint.1: Use the words 'some' and 'all' and write it split into two sentences.
y-m-53-07.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. Being equal at a few values is ..., and to say they are equal for all x, ...
y-m-53-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say why even a single value that does not match, like x=2, breaks 'equal for all x'?
y-m-53-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that to show 'equal for all x,' you need a different kind of evidence besides a few examples (such as rewriting the expressions into the same form)?
y-m-53-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Do you also know the cases where examples help (finding a counterexample)?
y-m-53-07.s.s3.model.0: Being equal at a few values is something confirmed only within the tested values, and being equal for all x means it must also be right for the values not yet put in. If even one value like x=2 does not match, it breaks, so a few is not enough.
y-m-53-07.s.s3.model.1: Being equal at some values does not mean being equal for all x. To say they are equal for all x, you have to show it by rewriting the expressions into the same form or explain that there is no value that does not match.

y-m-53-08.title: Designing inequalities whose solution is x>3
y-m-53-08.topic: Linear inequalities: designing inequalities with a given solution
y-m-53-08.goal: Learn that the sign of the coefficient decides the direction of the solution, design several linear inequalities with a given solution, and state the reason for the impossible case.
y-m-53-08.material: a, b, c are integers and a is not 0. x is a real number. When you solve the linear inequality ax+b<c, the solution comes out in the form 'x>some number' or 'x<some number.'
y-m-53-08.thinking.0: Making several answers within the conditions
y-m-53-08.thinking.1: Understanding how the direction of the inequality sign changes when multiplying or dividing by a negative number
y-m-53-08.thinking.2: Saying that something is impossible together with the reason
y-m-53-08.prereq.0: This assumes basic high school math learning (a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations). H1 is only a difficulty and support level for production assignment; it does not mean the curriculum places this subject in Grade 10, and school arrangements vary.
y-m-53-08.prereq.1: Solving linear inequalities (when you may add or multiply the same number on both sides, and the direction of the inequality sign)
y-m-53-08.prereq.2: Showing the solution of an inequality on a number line
y-m-53-08.s.s1.prompt: What is the appropriate solution of the inequality −2x+1<−5?
y-m-53-08.s.s1.hint.0: Put one value inside the range you think is the solution and one value outside it into the original inequality and check whether it holds.
y-m-53-08.s.s1.hint.1: Look at the relation between the direction in which −2x gets smaller and the direction in which x gets larger.
y-m-53-08.s.s1.r.a: Check what happens to the direction of the inequality sign when you divide both sides by a negative number.
y-m-53-08.s.s1.r.b: Check again the sign of the value of −6 divided by −2.
y-m-53-08.s.s1.r.c: You can check the result by putting 4 in for x and checking whether the inequality holds.
y-m-53-08.s.s1.r.d: Put x=−4 into the inequality and check whether it holds.
y-m-53-08.s.s1.explain: From −2x+1<−5 we get −2x<−6, and dividing by the negative number −2 reverses the inequality sign, so x>3. Putting in x=4 gives −8+1=−7<−5, which holds, and putting in x=2 gives −3<−5, which is false, so it does not hold.
y-m-53-08.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different inequalities ax+b<c whose solution is exactly x>3, and enter a, b, c. (a, b, c are integers. The absolute value of a is 10 or less, of b is 20 or less, and of c is 100 or less)
y-m-53-08.s.s2.hint.0: First find one a, b, c for which the solution of ax+b=c is 3.
y-m-53-08.s.s2.hint.1: Check what happens to the direction of the inequality sign when you solve ax+b<c with those a, b, c, and put in one value to check that the solution is x>3.
y-m-53-08.s.s2.ok.c1: It fits the range and the integer conditions.
y-m-53-08.s.s2.fail.c1: a, b, c must be integers with a≠0, |a|≤10, |b|≤20, |c|≤100.
y-m-53-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The coefficient of x is negative.
y-m-53-08.s.s2.fail.c2: With this a, the direction of the solution cannot be x>3. Think about the case where the direction of the inequality sign changes.
y-m-53-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The boundary of the solution is not 3. Adjust a, b, c so that the x satisfying ax+b=c is 3.
y-m-53-08.s.s2.explain: From ax+b<c we get ax<c−b, and if a<0, dividing both sides by a reverses the inequality sign, so x>(c−b)/a. We just need (c−b)/a=3. Examples: −x<−3, −2x+1<−5, −3x+2<−7.
y-m-53-08.s.s3.prompt: Can you make the solution x>3 with an inequality ax+b<c in which the coefficient a of x is positive? Write whether it is possible or not and the reason.
y-m-53-08.s.s3.hint.0: Pick one inequality with a positive a, like a=2, b=1, c=7, solve it directly, and check the direction of the solution.
y-m-53-08.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether the solution comes out in the same direction for a few other inequalities with positive a.
y-m-53-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say what happens to the direction of the inequality sign when you divide both sides by a when a is positive?
y-m-53-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check it with a concrete example (such as 2x+1<7)?
y-m-53-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Do you know that it is possible with another inequality sign such as ax+b>c?
y-m-53-08.s.s3.model.0: It is impossible. If a is positive, then dividing both sides by a keeps the direction of the inequality sign, so it takes the form x<(c−b)/a, and a solution like x>3 does not come out.
y-m-53-08.s.s3.model.1: It can't be done. If a>0, the solution has the form x<some number, which is the opposite direction from x>3, which goes on endlessly to the right. For example, 2x+1<7 gives x<3.
y-m-53-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: It would be even better to add that if you change the sign to >, it is possible even with a>0.

y-m-53-09.title: Leaving exactly three integer solutions
y-m-53-09.topic: Systems of linear inequalities: controlling the number of integer solutions
y-m-53-09.goal: Confirm that the number of integer solutions changes depending on whether the two ends of the interval are included, and design several systems of inequalities with exactly 3 integer solutions.
y-m-53-09.material: x is a real number. With two numbers p and q (p<q), make the system of inequalities 'x≥p and x<q,' that is, p≤x<q. (p is included and q is not included.) Pay attention to the number of integers x that fall in this range.
y-m-53-09.thinking.0: Looking at how including or excluding the boundary affects the count
y-m-53-09.thinking.1: Making several answers within the conditions
y-m-53-09.thinking.2: Explaining how the count changes when the boundary changes
y-m-53-09.prereq.0: This assumes basic high school math learning (a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations). H1 is only a difficulty and support level for production assignment; it does not mean the curriculum places this subject in Grade 10, and school arrangements vary.
y-m-53-09.prereq.1: Showing the solution of an inequality on a number line
y-m-53-09.prereq.2: A system of inequalities is the range of numbers that satisfy both inequalities at the same time
y-m-53-09.s.s1.prompt: When p=1, q=4, what are the integers x that satisfy the system 1≤x<4?
y-m-53-09.s.s1.hint.0: Mark 1 and 4 on the number line and distinguish them with a filled dot and an empty dot.
y-m-53-09.s.s1.hint.1: List the integers in the range from smallest and check whether the values at the two ends are included.
y-m-53-09.s.s1.r.a: Read the inequality sign '<' again to see whether the endpoint 4 is in the range.
y-m-53-09.s.s1.r.b: Read the inequality sign '≥' again to see whether the starting point 1 is included.
y-m-53-09.s.s1.r.c: List directly whether there are integers between 1 and 4.
y-m-53-09.s.s1.r.d: You read the inequality sign at each end and told apart whether it is included.
y-m-53-09.s.s1.explain: Since x≥1, 1 is included, and since x<4, 4 is not included. The integer solutions are the three integers 1, 2, 3.
y-m-53-09.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 pairs (p, q) such that exactly 3 integers satisfy p≤x<q and the 3 pairs have different sets of integer solutions. (p<q, and p and q are numbers from −50 to 50; decimals are allowed. Pairs with the same set of integer solutions count as the same example.)
y-m-53-09.s.s2.hint.0: First decide three consecutive integers, then decide p and q so that those three fall in the range while the integers just before and after are left out.
y-m-53-09.s.s2.hint.1: After deciding p and q, list the integers in the range directly and count whether there are exactly 3.
y-m-53-09.s.s2.ok.c1: p<q and they are within the range.
y-m-53-09.s.s2.fail.c1: p must be less than q, and both must be from −50 to 50.
y-m-53-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of integers in p≤x<q is not 3. List the integers in the range directly and count them.
y-m-53-09.s.s2.explain: If p=1, q=4, they are 1, 2, 3; if p=1.5, q=4.5, they are 2, 3, 4. If p=−2, q=1, they are −2, −1, 0. p=0.5, q=3.5 has the same set of integer solutions as p=1, q=4, so it is counted as one.
y-m-53-09.s.s3.prompt: In the system with p=1, q=4, if only the second inequality is changed to 'x≤4' (4 included), write what the integer solutions become and say the reason.
y-m-53-09.s.s3.hint.0: Change the point at 4 on the number line from an empty dot to a filled dot and list the integers in the range again.
y-m-53-09.s.s3.hint.1: Write the lists of integers before and after the change side by side and find where they differ.
y-m-53-09.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If we change it to x≤4, ...
y-m-53-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say which integer is newly included?
y-m-53-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you compare the cases where the difference between '<' and '≤' changes the count and where it does not (for example q=4.5)?
y-m-53-09.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Can you ask the same question about one of the examples you made in s2?
y-m-53-09.s.s3.model.0: If it becomes x≤4, then 4 is also included, so the integer solutions are 1, 2, 3, 4, which is 4. The count differs depending on whether the endpoint is included.
y-m-53-09.s.s3.model.1: If an equals sign is attached, the end value 4 is also a solution, so there are four. All the integers from 1 to 4 are included, so it goes up by one from 3.

y-m-53-10.title: Will giving many examples finish the explanation?
y-m-53-10.topic: Explanations using letters: checking examples and explaining for all integers
y-m-53-10.goal: Pick out the writing that completely explains the claim 'the product of two consecutive integers is even,' fill in the missing case yourself, and rewrite it as an explanation that can make a friend understand.
y-m-53-10.material: n is an integer. Claim: “The product n(n+1) of two consecutive integers is always even.” Four students explained this claim. Explanation ㄱ: For n=1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, the products were 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, 42, 56, 72, all even. We checked as many as eight, so it is always even. Explanation ㄴ: If n is even, let n=2k; then n(n+1)=2k(2k+1). It has a factor of 2, so it is even. Therefore it is always even. Explanation ㄷ: One of n and n+1 is always a multiple of 2, so the product is also a multiple of 2, that is, even. Explanation ㄹ: If n is even, n=2k and n(n+1)=2k(2k+1). If n is odd, let n+1=2k; then n(n+1)=2kn. Either way it is a multiple of 2, so it is even.
y-m-53-10.thinking.0: Telling apart checking examples and a general explanation
y-m-53-10.thinking.1: Finding the missing case in a case split
y-m-53-10.thinking.2: Rewriting an explanation to suit the reader
y-m-53-10.prereq.0: This assumes basic high school math learning (a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations). H1 is only a difficulty and support level for production assignment; it does not mean the curriculum places this subject in Grade 10, and school arrangements vary.
y-m-53-10.prereq.1: Writing even numbers as 2k and odd numbers as 2k+1 (k is an integer)
y-m-53-10.prereq.2: The basics of working with expressions that contain letters
y-m-53-10.s.s1.prompt: Pick all the explanations that show the claim holds for any integer n.
y-m-53-10.s.s1.hint.0: For each explanation, write in one line which n it covers (all integers or only some).
y-m-53-10.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the explanation carries over as it is when n is odd.
y-m-53-10.s.s1.r.a: This explanation puts n and n+1 together and deals with all integers at once using the properties of even and odd numbers. Even if it is short, look at whether the evidence follows through.
y-m-53-10.s.s1.r.b: Even if the number of checked values grows, it does not become an explanation for the numbers not checked. The standard is not how many were checked but whether all cases were covered.
y-m-53-10.s.s1.r.c: It dealt only with the case where n is even. It did not deal separately with the case where n is odd.
y-m-53-10.s.s1.r.d: This explanation splits into the two cases, even and odd, and covers all integers without leaving any out.
y-m-53-10.s.s1.explain: Explanations ㄷ and ㄹ cover every integer n. ㄷ does it by the fact that one of n and n+1 is a multiple of 2, and ㄹ does it by splitting into the two cases, even and odd. ㄱ is only a few checked numbers and does not cover every n, and ㄴ does not deal with the case where n is odd.
y-m-53-10.s.s2.prompt: A student continued Explanation ㄴ by writing the missing 'odd' case as below. Pick the wrong line.
y-m-53-10.s.s2.hint.0: Put values like 1 and 2 in for k and actually calculate (2k+1)·2(k+1).
y-m-53-10.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the values you calculated are even or odd, and compare them with the statement in line 4.
y-m-53-10.s.s2.line.0: If n is odd, let n=2k+1 (k is an integer).
y-m-53-10.s.s2.line.3: The product of an odd number (2k+1) and an even number 2(k+1) is odd, so it is not even.
y-m-53-10.s.s2.explain: In line 4, the product of an even and an odd number is even, not odd. (2k+1)·2(k+1) has a factor of 2, so it is even. Lines 1 to 3 are right. For example, if k=1, then 3×4=12, which is even.
y-m-53-10.s.s3.prompt: Fill in the missing case of Explanation ㄴ and continue the explanation so that a friend can understand 'why that case is also even.'
y-m-53-10.s.s3.hint.0: When n is odd, check with a few values whether n+1 is even or odd.
y-m-53-10.s.s3.hint.1: Write odd and even numbers with letters (the 2k form) and write the product.
y-m-53-10.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. We also need to look at the case where n is .... If we let ..., then ...
y-m-53-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does my explanation cover all cases where n is odd (using a letter, not by giving one example)?
y-m-53-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write it so that a friend reading it for the first time can tell which part is even?
y-m-53-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about whether it can be shortened into a more concise explanation like ㄷ?
y-m-53-10.s.s3.model.0: The case where n is odd is missing. If we let n=2k+1, then n+1=2k+2=2(k+1), so n(n+1)=(2k+1)·2(k+1), which has a factor of 2, so it is even. So the product is even when n is odd too.
y-m-53-10.s.s3.model.1: We need to look at the odd case too. If n is odd, then n+1 is even, so n(n+1) contains the even factor n+1, and an even number times any integer is even, so the product is even too.
y-m-53-10.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that explains using the fact that there is an even factor, without setting n+1=2k, is also valid.
